title: Topological bases and the lower-limit topology
section: Point-Set Topology ▷ Basis for a Topology
terms: basis; basis element; generated topology; lower-limit topology; Sorgenfrey line; second countable space.

exposition.text:
A basis covers the space and satisfies a local intersection condition: if x ∈ B ∩B , a basis element
1 2
B contains x and lies in that intersection. All unions of basis elements form the generated
3
topology. To compare two bases, test whether every point of each coarse basis element has a
fine basis element inside it.
Intervals (a, b) generate the usual topology on R, whereas [a, b) generate the lower-limit topol-
ogy. The latter is strictly finer. Its intervals [a, b) are both open and closed, and no subset
containing two distinct points is connected. Neighborhoods there control approach from the
right.
The usual real topology has a countable basis of rational-endpoint open intervals. The lower-
limit topology has no countable basis: refining [x, x + 1) at each real x requires distinct basis
elements with minimum x. A space with a countable basis is called second countable. In the
lower-limit line, any two points are separated within their subspace by complementary open
rays, so connected subsets contain at most one point.

question.text:
In the lower-limit topology on R, which sequence converges to 0?
n n
(A) x = −1/n (B) x = (−1) /n (C) x = 1/n (D) x = −1 (E) x = (−1)
n n n n n

solution.text:
Every basic neighborhood [0, ε) eventually contains 1/n. Each of the other sequences
has infinitely many negative terms or remains away from zero, and therefore fails the
neighborhood criterion.

Every right-hand neighborhood of 0 meets A, but [1, 1 + ε) misses it. Thus the closure is
[0, 1). The interior remains (0, 1), leaving boundary {0}.

question.text:
Which families are bases for the usual topology on R?
I. Open intervals with rational endpoints.
II. All open intervals of length one.
III. All closed intervals [a, b] with a < b.
(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and II only (D) I and III only (E) All three

solution.text:
Rational endpoints give intervals refining every ordinary neighborhood, and the local in-
tersection condition follows by choosing rational endpoints within an overlap. II fails that
condition when two length-one intervals overlap in an interval shorter than one. III fails
where two closed intervals meet only at one endpoint: no positive-length closed interval fits
inside that singleton.

question.text:
In the lower-limit topology on R, which description of [0, 1) is correct?
(A) Open, closed, and connected
(B) Open, closed, and disconnected
(C) Open but not closed, and connected
(D) Closed but not open, and disconnected
(E) Neither open nor closed

solution.text:
The interval is basic open. Its complement (−∞, 0) ∪ [1, ∞) is also a union of basic in-
tervals, so it is closed. But [0, 1/2) and [1/2, 1) form a disjoint, nonempty, relatively open
separation. Ordinary interval connectedness does not carry over to this finer topology.

question.text:
What can be said about the size of a basis for the lower-limit topology on R?
(A) A finite basis exists.
(B) A countably infinite basis exists.
(C) Every basis is uncountable.
(D) Every basis consists only of the intervals [a, b).
(E) No basis exists.

solution.text:
For each real x, a basis must supply B with x ∈ B ⊆ [x, x + 1). Such a set has minimum
x x
x, so the chosen sets for distinct x are distinct. There must therefore be at least as many
basis elements as real numbers. Rational left endpoints cannot refine a basic neighborhood
beginning at an irrational point.
